lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why we retell stories
lead.head: Once upon the same time

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 69

body: Picture a pre­his­toric human with no clothes, no cell­phone and no in­ter­net. A bright or­ange ob­ject rises and falls in the sky, day after day, and he has no idea what is going on. What does he do?
“You make up a story about it,” Amit Varma said, “and thus you have sun gods, and thus you have the be­gin­ning of re­li­gion.” {069-S01}
Storytelling, Varma ar­gued, is the first human in­stinct. The world is deeply com­plex, every story sim­pli­fies it, and with­out sto­ries we would be paral­ysed into in­ac­tion.

Ajay Shah agreed. Science and amuse­ment are both sto­ries, he said, on a spec­trum of how fan­ci­ful and how con­nected to re­al­ity. “We are not ro­bots, we’re not com­put­ers, we are not LLMs, we’re human.”
Then came the ques­tion be­hind the episode. We seem to tell an in­fi­nite num­ber of sto­ries. Why do we tell the ones we do?
## Only seven plots
Varma took his an­swer from a book he read many years back, Christopher Booker’s *The Seven Basic Plots*. Its claim is that there are only so many sto­ry­lines, and we fit ev­ery­thing into them.

So *Beowulf* and the *Epic of Gilgamesh*, *Jaws* and the James Bond films, and *Sholay* are “all ba­si­cally the same story”, Varma said. “They might seem com­pletely dif­fer­ent, but you’ve changed set­tings, you’ve changed char­ac­ters.” {069-C02}

The seven are Overcoming the Monster, Rags to Riches, the Quest, Voyage and Return, Comedy, Tragedy and Rebirth. They blend into one an­other. *The Lord of the Rings* and the Mahabharata, Varma said, con­tain all seven.

Booker gives each its own five acts. Underneath, Varma said, the shape is con­stant: “You start in a quiet place and then shit hap­pens and then you end in a quiet place.” The end can be death or hap­pi­ness.
## A struc­ture, not a cage
Varma was care­ful not to be pre­scrip­tive. Modern lit­er­a­ture and cin­ema go be­yond these plots, he told writ­ers, and they should fol­low their hearts.
Formula is real enough. Sturgeon’s Law, he said, holds that 95 per cent of ev­ery­thing is crap, and stu­dio ex­ec­u­tives try to force tem­plates on film­mak­ers.

But the an­swer, Varma ar­gued, is not to aban­don form. “The way to break out of medi­ocrity is not to break out of the struc­ture. It is to do in­ter­est­ing things within the struc­ture and make it work for you.” {069-C04}
## Whose story is it?
Which plot a story fol­lows can de­pend on whose eyes you see it through. Give Goliath a back­story, Varma said, and David and Goliath be­comes a tragedy. {069-C09}
A live war is a plot whose genre is not yet set­tled. Shah cast the Battle of Kyiv as Overcoming the Monster; Varma warned that it could still end as tragedy.

Varma closed with a pas­sage from Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn’s *The Gulag Archipelago*, which Booker quotes at the start of his chap­ter on re­birth. The line be­tween good and evil, it says, runs through every human heart, and it moves over time. {069-C13}
Then it started rain­ing. “We are not in a stu­dio with green screen,” Varma said, and the hosts would have to rush back in­side. First, though, he made a plea.
Stories have to sim­plify, he said, often into black and white. The real world is com­pli­cated. “Let us not rush to judg­ment. Let us not think we are good and oth­ers are evil.”
Within all of us, Varma said, are hero and vil­lain, com­edy and tragedy, David and Goliath. The sto­ries he would love sto­ry­tellers to tell are ones that em­brace this com­plex­ity.

second.label: Overcoming the monster
second.head: Kyiv’s unfinished script
second.deck: Ajay Shah casts the Battle of Kyiv as Booker’s first plot

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Battle of Kyiv

body: Life in Ukraine was nor­mal until a mon­ster in­vaded from the north, Ajay Shah said, re­call­ing the Battle of Kyiv from the hosts’ episodes on sto­ries that should be films. The world, Shah in­cluded, as­sumed Ukraine would fall. {069-S05}

Then the scrappy Ukrainians, armed with ar­tillery and Javelin mis­siles, stopped the mon­ster in his tracks. Amit Varma promised to buy Shah a kurta and a pa­tiala “be­cause there is an artist in you”. {069-J03}

Varma mapped it onto the mon­ster plot’s five acts: the call, ini­tial suc­cess, con­fronta­tion, final or­deal, mirac­u­lous es­cape. But this is the real world, he added. The end­ing is un­writ­ten, and it could yet be a tragedy.

quote.text: It’s only a ques­tion of when Ukraine will be con­quered, not whether, and my­self in­cluded.

third.head: Scrooge on a slow train

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Amrish Puri’s rebirth

body: Ajay Shah has seen few films, but he has seen *Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge*. What he re­mem­bers is the last scene: the slow train at an ob­scure sta­tion, a feel­ing any­one who has made such jour­neys knows. {#slowtrain}
Amit Varma used the film twice. First it served as voy­age and re­turn, a jour­ney from which the trav­ellers come back changed. Then he went back to its cli­max: “Ja Simran, jee le apni zindagi”.
What mat­ters there, Varma said, is what hap­pens to the stern fa­ther played by Amrish Puri. “He changes. He is re­born.” {069-S10}

Varma com­pared him to Scrooge in Dickens’ *A Christmas Carol*. Change hap­pens in every plot, he said, but in a re­birth story it is the whole point: some­one be­comes a fun­da­men­tally dif­fer­ent per­son. {069-C11}

p2.deck: Christopher Booker’s *The Seven Basic Plots*, plot by plot, as Amit Varma read it and Ajay Shah tested it. {069-R01}

box.title: The book on the table
box.text: Christopher Booker’s *The Seven Basic Plots* ar­gues that every story re­cy­cles one of seven archetypes. Amit Varma read it many years back, calls it ex­cel­lent, and of­fers it as a lens for writ­ers, not a rule­book. {069-R01}

sections.label: The prologue
sections.head: One arc, many costumes
sections.caption: how Booker found his pattern
body: Christopher Booker no­ticed the pat­tern while read­ing sev­eral works at once. {#simultaneous} Among them were *Macbeth* and *Lolita*, and he watched Truffaut’s film *Jules et Jim*. The same thing, Amit Varma said, was hap­pen­ing in all of them.

Each be­gins with a hero who is in some way un­ful­filled, and a mood of an­tic­i­pa­tion. He finds a focus for his de­sires and en­joys dream­like suc­cess: Macbeth be­comes king, Humbert be­gins his af­fair with Lolita, Icarus dis­cov­ers he can fly, Faust gets the devil’s magic.

“But grad­u­ally the mood of the story dark­ens,” Booker writes. {069-S02} The dream turns into a night­mare and ends in vi­o­lent self-destruction. Varma said the same arc runs through *Romeo and Juliet* and *Madame Bovary*.
## Quiet, trou­ble, quiet
Anyone in Versova, Varma said, has no doubt tried writ­ing screen­plays, and knows Syd Field’s three-act struc­ture: set-up, con­flict, res­o­lu­tion. {069-J12}
Booker gives each archetype its own five acts. The acts dif­fer, but the shape holds: a quiet start, an up­heaval, a quiet end, whether in death or hap­pi­ness. {069-C03}

~ Ajay Shah won­dered whether each of the seven could be­come a thou­sand-word prompt for an LLM to mass-produce fic­tion. {#thousandword} A dreary use, he con­ceded, and not where Varma was. A lot of rub­bish writ­ing, he added, is al­ready being done with LLMs.

quote.text: Finally, seem­ingly in­ex­orably, the story works up to a cli­max of vi­o­lent self-destruction. The dream ends in death.
quote.who: Christopher Booker, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: The first plot
sections.head: Beowulf, meet the shark
sections.caption: overcoming the monster
body: The first archetype, Amit Varma an­nounced, is over­com­ing the Indian state. He was kid­ding. It is over­com­ing the mon­ster. {069-J01}
It runs from the *Epic of Gilgamesh* and *Beowulf* to the James Bond films, *Star Wars* and *Jaws*. Booker, Varma said, com­pares *Beowulf* with *Jaws* and finds them ba­si­cally the same story.
In India there are *Sholay* and *Krrish*. The mon­ster can be a human em­bod­i­ment or a lit­eral one, as in *Jurassic Park* or *King Kong*.

The arc is sim­ple: things are nor­mal, a mon­ster ar­rives, things go badly, and even­tu­ally we win. Unless, Varma added, the mon­ster is the Indian state, a film he does not think has been writ­ten yet.
## When we lose

Ajay Shah ob­jected that if the story ends in de­feat, it is not this type. Then it is tragedy, Varma replied. Story types merge, he said: *The Lord of the Rings* and Harry Potter both kill off a big mon­ster, but carry other arcs too.
Booker’s five acts for this plot are the call, ini­tial suc­cess, con­fronta­tion, final or­deal and mirac­u­lous es­cape, com­mon, Varma said, to all the James Bond films. {#fiveacts}
~ Ukraine fits so far, Varma said: Zelensky in his of­fice, some­thing hap­pens, then ini­tial suc­cess. But this is the real world. It is story type one or story type five, Shah said. {#typefive}

quote.text: Unless that mon­ster is a Indian state. I don’t think that film has been writ­ten yet.

sections.label: The third plot
sections.head: In search of number three
sections.caption: the quest
body: “Are you on a quest to find num­ber three?” Amit Varma asked. “Number three is a quest.” {069-J05}

You search for some­thing, go on a jour­ney and even­tu­ally find it. It is in many ways the old­est archetype, Varma said: the *Odyssey*, *Pilgrim’s Progress* and *The Divine Comedy* cen­tre on it, as do *Raiders of the Lost Ark*, *Finding Nemo* and *Chennai Express*.
Ajay Shah asked whether the Manhattan Project counted. Absolutely, said Varma, adding that the Oppenheimer story is also a tragedy. “I’m very good at iden­ti­fy­ing tragedy, you see.” {069-J06}

Shah’s pick was Tracy Kidder’s *The Soul of a New Machine*: a jour­nal­ist em­bed­ded at Data General as a team builds one CPU. It takes you into the minds of the en­gi­neers and their leader, Tom West, and the empti­ness after it is fin­ished. {069-R02}
## Five stages
The acts are the call, the jour­ney, ar­rival and frus­tra­tion, the final or­deal and the goal.

~ Varma read Shah’s own life as a quest. After IIT and a PhD in eco­nom­ics in the US, Shah chose to come back to India, when kids of his gen­er­a­tion saw get­ting out as es­cap­ing. The quest, to make India a bet­ter place, is on­go­ing. {069-S08}

quote.text: You made the call to come back, and the quest of course is make India a bet­ter place, and I guess that’s on­go­ing

sections.label: The fourth plot
sections.head: Gone to Goa, back changed
sections.caption: voyage and return
body: Ajay Shah com­plained that three plots in, there had not been enough ro­mance. {#romance} So Amit Varma asked him what DDLJ stood for.

The fourth archetype is voy­age and re­turn: you make a jour­ney, you come back, and usu­ally you come back changed. *Alice in Wonderland*, *Peter Pan*, *The Time Machine* and *Back to the Future* fit, Varma said, as do DDLJ, *Dil Chahta Hai*, with its trip to Goa, *Jab We Met* and *Queen*.
Why does it ap­peal? Many peo­ple feel stuck, Varma said, liv­ing what Thoreau called lives of quiet des­per­a­tion, and it is at­trac­tive to think that going some­where will change them. {069-J15}
Shah re­called a line he at­trib­uted to Robert McNamara: we go on the jour­ney, and when we come back we un­der­stand where we had been. {#mcnamara}
## Hobbit or ring?

The acts run from an­tic­i­pa­tion and ini­tial fas­ci­na­tion to frus­tra­tion, night­mare, and es­cape and re­turn. Varma’s idea of night­mare: a trek on which you break your leg and hang off a cliff, sure you will die.

~ Shah drew a fine line. *The Hobbit* be­longs here, he said: they go out on a fi­nite prob­lem, to slay a dragon, and come back changed. {#hobbit} Then they are ready for the quest, *The Lord of the Rings*, which is struc­turally dif­fer­ent.

quote.text: The zen you find at the top of the moun­tain is the zen that you take with your­self.

sections.label: The fifth plot
sections.head: No laugh track required
sections.caption: comedy as a structure
body: Comedy, in Christopher Booker’s sense, is not about mak­ing you laugh, Amit Varma said. It is a struc­ture: a lit­tle world under a shadow of con­fu­sion, a night­mar­ish tan­gle, then a rev­e­la­tion that brings ev­ery­one to­gether in joy­ful re­union. {#littleworld}

As a boy, Varma saw Shakespeare’s plays sorted into come­dies and tragedies, and took com­edy to mean what­ever made him laugh. But the genre runs on mis­un­der­stand­ings, mis­taken iden­ti­ties and con­fu­sion, all cleared up for a happy end­ing.

Booker lists four com­mon el­e­ments. Characters im­pris­oned in anger, greed or jeal­ousy must change, or be shown up. True iden­ti­ties are re­vealed. People find their other halves. Whatever was lost is re­stored.
## Love and laugh­ter part ways

Ajay Shah doubted that the form sur­vived in twen­ti­eth-century lit­er­a­ture: “we don’t take P. G. Wodehouse as se­ri­ous lit­er­a­ture”. Wodehouse, Varma replied, is one of its finest ex­am­ples, and Jane Austen’s *Pride and Prejudice*, *Sense and Sensibility* and *Emma* are come­dies in struc­ture. {069-J18}
In the twen­ti­eth cen­tury, Booker ar­gues, love and laugh­ter went their sep­a­rate ways. A rom-com may not have much laugh­ter, Varma said, and in *Housefull* ro­mance is not cen­tral. {069-C07}

~ Every Mills and Boon book fol­lows the struc­ture, Varma said. {069-J08} How to refer to thirty of them in the plu­ral, no­body could set­tle. Shah of­fered an eas­ier one: the plu­ral of Attorney General is Attorneys General.

quote.text: But now love and laugh­ter have kind of gone in dif­fer­ent di­rec­tions.

sections.label: The sixth plot
sections.head: Goliath’s side of the story
sections.caption: tragedy and point of view
body: Tragedy, Amit Varma said, fol­lows a noble pro­tag­o­nist lured into ig­no­ble acts until ev­ery­thing falls apart, usu­ally in death. The form runs from *Oedipus Rex* to *Macbeth*, *Hamlet* and *Julius Caesar*.

In *Julius Caesar*, he said, the tragedy is not Caesar’s but Brutus’s, a noble man who de­bases him­self. {#brutus} Ajay Shah likened the open­ing stage of an­tic­i­pa­tion to the warn­ing to be­ware the Ides of March.
*Bonnie and Clyde* and *Jules et Jim* fit, and in India *Devdas*, though of Sanjay Leela Bhansali’s ver­sion, Varma said, “the film it­self was a tragedy”. {069-J10}
## Whose eyes?
The genre de­pends on point of view. Give Goliath a back­story, Varma said, trapped in his image of strength, never hav­ing found love, and David and Goliath be­comes a tragedy. {069-C09}

In his writ­ing course, he asks stu­dents to retell a known story from an­other point of view. Some have told *Sholay* from Gabbar Singh’s side, or Harry Potter from Voldemort’s, with back­sto­ries in which the vil­lain is a vic­tim of cir­cum­stance. {069-S11}

~ Shah sug­gested the Mahabharata from Draupadi’s point of view. Varma called the epic a mas­ter­piece that sur­vives as mag­nif­i­cent sto­ry­telling, not only through re­li­gion. One of his favourite books of all time, Irawati Karve’s *Yuganta*, is can­did about its misog­yny.

quote.text: Maybe Goliath sees the stone com­ing from the cat­a­pult and he chooses to let it hit him.

Gradually it be­came clear to me that the line sep­a­rat­ing good from evil runs not be­tween states, not be­tween classes, and not be­tween par­ties. It runs through the heart of each and every one of us

p3.title: Told and retold
p3.deck: Four stories from the episode, and which of the seven plots each follows

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on two quests told side by side
stories.head: A quest that kept her awake
body: In one of the hosts’ episodes on sto­ries that should be films, Amit Varma told two sto­ries at once, decades apart, and both were quests. {#twoquests} Here he used them to il­lus­trate the third plot.
In one, Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan sets out to de­feat the British Empire, and then to make some­thing of the new na­tion. He suc­ceeds in the first quest, Varma said, and fails in the sec­ond.
In the other, Mukulika Banerjee goes to the Pathan areas of Pakistan to find sur­vivors of the Khudai Khidmatgar.

Her ques­tion was why “a peo­ple who are sup­posed to be vi­o­lent Pathans could take part in the great­est non­vi­o­lent move­ment of all time”, and lead it with orig­i­nal think­ing. {069-S09} Varma urged lis­ten­ers to read her book, *The Pathan Unarmed*.

Her call, in Booker’s terms, came from her PhD ad­viser, who told her to do a PhD only if some­thing kept her awake at night. {#awake} Then came the jour­ney, and the dif­fi­culty of find­ing sur­viv­ing mem­bers.
The final or­deal, Varma said, be­longed less to her than to Ghaffar Khan, whose free­dom move­ment had its arc and its low mo­ments. Then comes the goal, and the quest is over.

~ Ajay Shah had been well briefed. When Banerjee came to the XKDR Forum of­fice a cou­ple of months ear­lier, he said, “I smiled at her with an extra thou­sand words be­cause of all the things you told me.” {#programmed}
stories.why: A quest can end in vic­tory and heart­break at once, as Ghaffar Khan’s did. And the call need not be grand: some­times it is a sin­gle ques­tion about what keeps you awake at night.
stories.postscript: Varma also in­ter­viewed Banerjee for his pod­cast, *The Seen and the Unseen*, and told lis­ten­ers to hear that episode too.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Mukulika Banerjee’s quest

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the call that opens every quest
stories.head: Nanda Devi, on the house
body: When Amit Varma de­scribed the call that opens a quest, Ajay Shah re­mem­bered a story from one of their episodes: a plu­to­nium-powered de­vice meant to be mounted on top of Nanda Devi, in a mis­sion that went ter­ri­bly wrong.

What stayed with him was one para­graph. Quietly, one by one, the CIA ap­proached the world’s most elite climbers with an offer: climb Nanda Devi, all ex­penses paid. {069-S06} There was just one minor de­tail. “You’re gonna have to do some work for us.”

Shah’s own call was qui­eter. He was part of a project to climb Kokankada in the Sahyadris, and re­mem­bers vividly how its leader, Girish Sant, “took me aside one evening say­ing, Do you want to come on this?” {069-S07}
~ That, Shah said, is the great mo­ment: come, let’s go do it.
stories.why: The call to ad­ven­ture often ar­rives as an ir­re­sistible offer, with the catch in the small print. And in real life it is rarely dra­matic: one per­son qui­etly asks an­other whether they are in.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the CIA’s call to the climbers

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the second plot, rags to riches
stories.head: Keep your money, I’m Rocky
body: Amit Varma opened the sec­ond archetype with a quiz: what do Sylvester Stallone, Julia Roberts, Anne Hathaway and Ranbir Kapoor have in com­mon? {#quiz} Ajay Shah re­mem­bered a story Varma had told him: Stallone wrote *Rocky*.

He did, Varma said, and he wanted to act in it. The stu­dio of­fered a lot of money for the script, as long as some­one else played the part. Stallone’s reply, as Varma told it: “Fuck you I wanna act in it.” {069-S03}

*Rocky* is rags to riches, as are *Pretty Woman*, *The Devil Wears Prada* and *Rockstar*, and long be­fore them *Cinderella* and *Aladdin*. Most peo­ple dream of being much bet­ter off, Varma said, so it is a trope ev­ery­one can iden­tify with.
~ Varma did not count him­self among them. “My life sadly only rags,” he said. {069-J04}
stories.why: By turn­ing down the safe deal, Stallone made his own life a rags-to-riches story, the same plot as the film he would not give up. Varma called it quite bril­liant.

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s father, and a tease about the sequel
stories.head: From Hyderabad, Sindh, to CMIE
body: Rags to riches is not only for the movies. Asked by Amit Varma for his father’s story, Ajay Shah said it began in Hyderabad, Sindh, in what is now Pakistan, where there was just noth­ing around.
From there, his fa­ther ended up as “one of the cool econ­o­mists of the coun­try” and founded CMIE, “all in a short fifty eight years”. {069-S04}
Varma called it a beau­ti­ful story, then turned to the son. “Your story, will it be tragedy? Are you gonna let him down?” {#letdown} “Riches to rags,” came the an­swer.
~ Asked late in the episode whether he had ever been re­born, Shah said not in fun­da­men­tal ways. “Lots of im­ple­men­ta­tion de­tail has hap­pened, but the foun­da­tions were the same.” {069-J11}
stories.why: The archetype is not only for fairy tales: it de­scribes real lives. And one fam­ily can hold more than one plot, as Varma’s tease to the son showed within mo­ments.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on his father’s story

quiz.q: Which film did Christopher Booker compare with Beowulf, finding them basically the same story?
quiz.a: *Jaws*. Both are tales of over­com­ing the mon­ster, the first of the seven plots.

quiz.q: According to Sturgeon’s Law, as Amit Varma cited it, what share of everything is crap?
quiz.a: Ninety-five per cent, which is why so much for­mula writ­ing is medi­ocre.

quiz.q: What did the studio want from Sylvester Stallone, and what did he insist on?
quiz.a: To buy his *Rocky* script; he in­sisted on act­ing in it him­self.

quiz.q: In *Julius Caesar*, whose tragedy is it, according to Amit Varma?
quiz.a: Brutus’s, a noble man who de­bases him­self and suf­fers for it.

quiz.q: Which DDLJ character does Varma say is truly reborn, and which Dickens figure does he resemble?
quiz.a: The fa­ther played by Amrish Puri, com­pared to Scrooge in *A Christmas Carol*.

quiz.q: What did Varma say India had, thousands of years before open-source software?
quiz.a: An open-source epic: the Ramayana, re­told dif­fer­ently in every re­gion and era.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 69. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Sylvester Stallone (Georges Biard, CC BY-SA 3.0); P. G. Wodehouse (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Jane Austen (Cassandra Austen, public domain); Milan Kundera (Elisa Cabot, CC BY-SA 3.0); Tracy Kidder (Bill O’Donnell, CC BY-SA 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Open Library and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: The Soul of a New Machine
shelf.creator: Tracy Kidder
shelf.why: A jour­nal­ist em­bed­ded with a Data General team build­ing a CPU takes you into the minds of the en­gi­neers and their leader, Tom West, in­clud­ing the empti­ness once the quest was over.

shelf.title: The Pathan Unarmed
shelf.creator: Mukulika Banerjee
shelf.why: Ten years of field­work on how Pathan peas­ants, stereo­typed as vi­o­lent, built the subcontinent’s great­est non­vi­o­lent move­ment, the Khudai Khidmatgar: Bacha Khan rooted it in the inner jihad and the Pashtun codes of courage, hos­pi­tal­ity and refuge.

shelf.title: The Incredible Curiosities of Mukulika Banerjee (Episode 276, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Mukulika Banerjee’s re­search sto­ries: her fight for fund­ing and her field­work in the North-West Frontier Province hunt­ing for sur­viv­ing Khudai Khidmatgars, which Amit calls a clas­sic quest nar­ra­tive.

shelf.title: The ‘Stories That Should Be Films’ episodes of Everything is Everything (Episodes 23, 29 and 43)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The first of the show’s se­ries of true sto­ries the hosts would turn into films, and Amit’s favourite episode at the time.

shelf.title: Yuganta
shelf.creator: Irawati Karve
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite books: a bril­liant, some­times dis­qui­et­ing so­ci­o­log­i­cal read­ing of the Mahabharata and the role of women in it, can­did about its misog­yny, and an anal­y­sis of a so­ci­ety we still live in.

shelf.title: Three Hundred Ramayanas
shelf.creator: AK Ramanujan
shelf.why: Ramanujan’s essay shows the Ramayana con­stantly re­told across times and places, each ver­sion (tribal ones com­pletely dif­fer­ent) adapt­ing the epic to the so­ci­ety that told it.

shelf.title: Laughable Loves
shelf.creator: Milan Kundera
shelf.why: He calls it ‘a great book’ and ‘magnificent’.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

laughs.text: Amit in­tro­duces the first archetype as ‘over­com­ing the Indian state’, then ad­mits he is kid­ding. Later he says every mon­ster gets beaten in the end, ‘Unless that mon­ster is a Indian state. I don’t think that film has been writ­ten yet.’

Ajay pro­poses using LLM prompts to mass-produce fic­tion from the seven tem­plates, then clas­si­fy­ing a hun­dred Malayalam films by type to com­pute ‘means and variances’ of what works. He goes ‘all movie executive’: ‘No, dude, you’re going to go down line of at­tack num­ber two.’ Amit replies: ‘I am the artist... He’s the suit, though you’re not wear­ing a suit, but it’s close enough.’

Amit on spot­ting Oppenheimer as a tragedy: ‘I’m very good at iden­ti­fy­ing tragedy, you see... The world is filled with tragedy, and also I think my gaze is filled with tragedy, but it is what it is.’
Amit lists Devdas as a tragedy: ‘Though if it is the... Sanjay Leela Bhansali Devdas, I think the film it­self was a tragedy, but we shall uh leave that aside.’
Sturgeon’s Law, ‘95% of ev­ery­thing is crap’, in­voked to ex­plain why so much for­mula writ­ing is medi­ocre.
Robert Pirsig, quoted by Ajay: ‘The zen you find at the top of the moun­tain is the zen that you take with your­self.’
